entities.summary:
Dacius, Archbishop of Milan from approximately 530 CE until his death in 552 CE, was a pivotal ecclesiastical leader during the tumultuous Gothic Wars that reshaped the Italian peninsula. His episcopate coincided with the final collapse of Ostrogothic rule and the Byzantine reconquest under Emperor Justinian I, making him a central figure in the religious and political landscape of early 6th-century Italy. Dacius is primarily remembered for his unwavering commitment to Nicene Orthodoxy against Arianism and his spirited defense of the Three Chapters, a theological controversy that deeply divided the Christian world and challenged papal authority.

During his tenure, Dacius played a critical role in resisting the Arian Ostrogothic kings, particularly Theodahad and Witiges, who viewed orthodox bishops with suspicion. When Witiges besieged Rome in 537–538 CE, Dacius journeyed to Constantinople, seeking imperial intervention and advocating for the Italian Church. Later, he accompanied the Byzantine general Belisarius during the reconquest, demonstrating the close alliance between the Catholic hierarchy and imperial power. His presence at the Council of Constantinople in 536 CE, where he condemned Monophysitism, further solidified his reputation as a staunch defender of Chalcedonian Christology, even as he later found himself at odds with Justinian over the condemnation of the Three Chapters.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Dacius's firm stance against Arianism and his resistance to imperial theological dictates during the Gothic Wars helped preserve Nicene Orthodoxy in Milan and influenced the complex relationship between the papacy and the Byzantine Empire, impacting the future of the Western Church.
